segments.t: Drinking alone in Susukino, Sapporo's lively entertainment district, Muranishi witnesses a loud argument over twenty thousand yen. After the bar's Mama-san restores order, a young hustler named Toshi sits down beside Muranishi to thank him and pour a drink. Listen to their first meeting.
何を返すんだよ？二万？
二人ともやめなさい！
次に騒ぎを起こしたら、トシちゃん、追い出すからね。
分かってるよ、ママ。
悪かったって。ママ、今日も美しいね。
あんたもね。はいはい。
俺はトシだ。助かったよ。
まあ、一杯やってくれよ。
いや、もう十分だ。
そんな冷たいこと言うなよ。
さあ、グラスを持ってきて。
じゃあ、少しだけいただくよ。
Bar banter moves fast—from stern scolding to shameless flattery to pouring drinks. Let's unpack each expression.
何を返すんだよ？二万？

'Give back what? Twenty thousand yen?' "Kaesu" means to return something to its owner. Notice Japanese counts big sums in units of "man", ten thousand—so "niman" is two ten-thousands, twenty thousand!
二人ともやめなさい！
'Both of you, stop it right now!' "Futari tomo" addresses the pair together as 'both of you'. Attaching "nasai" to "yameru", to stop, gives Mama-san a firm motherly command.
次に騒ぎを起こしたら、トシちゃん、追い出すからね。

'Cause a commotion next time, Toshi-chan, and I will throw you out.' "Tsugi ni" means next time, "sawagi" is a ruckus, and "oidasu" joins "ou", chase, with "dasu", put out—literally 'chase out the door'.
ママ、今日も美しいね。
'Mama, you look beautiful today too.' Turning on the charm, Toshi uses "kyou mo", today as well, and literary-sounding "utsukushii", beautiful.
あんたもね。はいはい。
'You too, sure, sure.' Not fooled by his flattery, Mama-san brushes him off with "hai hai"—saying "hai" twice in a row means 'yeah, yeah, whatever you say'.
助かったよ。
'You really helped me out.' Literally "tasukatta" means 'I was saved!'—the everyday way Japanese speakers thank someone whenever a small favour rescues them from a tight spot.
まあ、一杯やってくれよ。
'Come on, let me pour you a drink.' "Ippai" counts one cup or glass, and "ippai yaru" is relaxed after-work shorthand for having a drink together.
いや、もう十分だ。
'No, I have had plenty already.' "Mou juubun" pairs "mou", already, with "juubun", enough or plenty—useful whenever someone tries to refill your glass or plate.
そんな冷たいこと言うなよ。
'Do not say something so cold.' Just as English calls an unfriendly refusal 'cold', Japanese uses "tsumetai", chilly to the touch, for a cold attitude.
さあ、グラスを持ってきて。
'Come on, bring a glass over here.' Combining "motte", holding, with "kite", come, gives "motte kite"—'bring it here!' Now let's listen to Toshi and Muranishi's bar meeting again.
何を返すんだよ？二万？
二人ともやめなさい！
次に騒ぎを起こしたら、トシちゃん、追い出すからね。
分かってるよ、ママ。
悪かったって。ママ、今日も美しいね。
あんたもね。はいはい。
俺はトシだ。助かったよ。
まあ、一杯やってくれよ。
いや、もう十分だ。
そんな冷たいこと言うなよ。
さあ、グラスを持ってきて。
じゃあ、少しだけいただくよ。
Keep "tasukatta" handy for 'you saved me!', "mou juubun" when you have had enough, and "motte kite" to ask someone to bring something over. See you in scene twenty-six.
またね。
